name: Scholarships and Scams
title: Scholarships and Scams
answer: Scholarship searches can help students pay for college, and AI can help them organize applications and deadlines, but scholarship scams are a real risk. Students and families should never pay to apply for a scholarship or share sensitive financial information with an unknown organization, and every scholarship should be verified through a counselor or an official source before applying.

sections.body: This idea is about helping students find legitimate scholarship money while avoiding fraud. Scholarship searches, including BigFuture and state aid websites, can connect students with awards, and counselors can help students identify the ones that fit them. AI can assist with organizing applications and deadlines, but the student still writes each application in their own words. The problem it solves is twofold: students may miss available aid, and they may fall for services that charge fees, promise guaranteed awards, or collect personal information through fake scholarships. AI tools can make the second problem worse by producing convincing fake websites and messages.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: In a school or classroom, counselors help students use scholarship searches and point them to awards that match their situation. Students use AI to keep track of applications and deadlines, while writing each application themselves in their own words. Counselors warn families every year about the warning signs of scholarship scams, including fees to find scholarships, guaranteed awards, and requests for sensitive financial information from unknown organizations. Schools can keep a list of verified scholarships and update it regularly, which protects families and saves students time. Before applying, students verify any scholarship through their counselor or an official source. The text does not give grade band variations for this idea.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The text gives no study, figure, or finding for this idea, and it does not carry an evidence label. It rests on practice and on the stated experience that scholarship scams are a real risk and that AI tools can make them worse by producing convincing fake websites and messages. The recommendation to keep a verified list is presented as a practical protection for families and a time saver for students, not as a research result.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The limits and risks are clear in the text. Students and families should never pay to apply for a scholarship or share sensitive financial information with an unknown organization. Some services charge fees to find scholarships or promise guaranteed awards, and some fake scholarships collect personal information. AI tools can make scams worse by producing convincing fake websites and messages, so students should verify any scholarship through their counselor or an official source before applying. The decisions that stay with people are the verification of each scholarship, the yearly warning to families, and the keeping of a regularly updated list of verified scholarships. The student also stays responsible for writing each application in their own words.
